questions.question: State the order of these substances from most to least reactive: potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, carbon, zinc, iron, hydrogen and copper.
questions.modelAnswer: K, Na, Li, Ca, Mg, Al, carbon, Zn, Fe, hydrogen, Cu. Carbon and hydrogen are reference positions used to predict extraction and reactions with acids.
markingPoints: K, Na, Li, Ca, Mg, Al, carbon, Zn, Fe, hydrogen, Cu. Carbon and hydrogen are reference positions used to predict extraction and reactions with acids.

questions.question: Use the reactivity series to predict the reactions of potassium, magnesium, zinc and copper with water and with dilute hydrochloric acid. Include products and typical observations.
questions.modelAnswer: K reacts violently with cold water → KOH + H₂. Mg reacts very slowly with cold water but with steam → MgO + H₂; reacts with acid giving MgCl₂ + H₂. Zn does not react significantly with cold water but reacts with steam and acid → ZnO/ZnCl₂ + H₂. Cu does not react with water or dilute HCl because below hydrogen. Observations can include fizzing, metal disappearing, temperature rise.
markingPoints: K reacts violently with cold water → KOH + H₂. Mg reacts very slowly with cold water but with steam → MgO + H₂

reacts with acid giving MgCl₂ + H₂. Zn does not react significantly with cold water but reacts with steam and acid → ZnO/ZnCl₂ + H₂. Cu does not react with water or dilute HCl because below hydrogen. Observations can include fizzing, metal disappearing, temperature rise.

questions.question: A strip of zinc is placed in copper sulfate solution, and copper is placed in magnesium sulfate solution. Predict observations, write equations and explain both outcomes.
questions.modelAnswer: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. Zinc is more reactive, so displaces Cu²⁺; blue solution fades and brown copper coats zinc. Cu + MgSO₄: no reaction because copper is less reactive than magnesium and cannot displace Mg²⁺.
markingPoints: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. Zinc is more reactive, so displaces Cu²⁺
blue solution fades and brown copper coats zinc. Cu + MgSO₄: no reaction because copper is less reactive than magnesium and cannot displace Mg²⁺.

questions.question: For Mg + CuO → MgO + Cu, identify what is oxidised and reduced using both oxygen transfer and electron transfer. Write the ionic electron changes.
questions.modelAnswer: Mg gains oxygen and is oxidised; CuO loses oxygen and is reduced. Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ is oxidation (loss of electrons). Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu is reduction (gain of electrons). OIL RIG.
markingPoints: Mg gains oxygen and is oxidised
CuO loses oxygen and is reduced. Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ is oxidation (loss of electrons). Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu is reduction (gain of electrons). OIL RIG.

questions.question: Explain how a metal’s position relative to carbon determines its extraction method. Apply this to aluminium, zinc, iron, copper and gold.
questions.modelAnswer: Metals below carbon can be reduced from oxides by carbon/carbon monoxide: zinc and iron. Metals above carbon, including aluminium, require electrolysis of molten compounds because carbon cannot reduce them. Copper may be reduced with carbon or obtained by biological/chemical methods. Very unreactive gold can occur native. Electrolysis is expensive because it uses much electricity.
markingPoints: Metals below carbon can be reduced from oxides by carbon/carbon monoxide: zinc and iron. Metals above carbon, including aluminium, require electrolysis of molten compounds because carbon cannot reduce them. Copper may be reduced with carbon or obtained by biological/chemical methods. Very unreactive gold can occur native. Electrolysis is expensive because it uses much electricity.

questions.question: Compare bioleaching and phytomining for extracting copper from low-grade ores, including how copper is recovered and environmental/economic advantages and disadvantages.
questions.modelAnswer: Bioleaching uses bacteria to produce a solution containing copper ions; recover by displacement with iron or electrolysis. Phytomining: plants absorb copper ions, are harvested/burned and copper is recovered from ash. Both use low-grade ores, reduce quarrying/energy and can work on waste; both are slow, require land/control, may produce toxic solutions/gases, and often need further processing.
markingPoints: Bioleaching uses bacteria to produce a solution containing copper ions

recover by displacement with iron or electrolysis. Phytomining: plants absorb copper ions, are harvested/burned and copper is recovered from ash. Both use low-grade ores, reduce quarrying/energy and can work on waste
both are slow, require land/control, may produce toxic solutions/gases, and often need further processing.

questions.question: Define an acid and an alkali in terms of ions in aqueous solution. State what happens to H⁺ concentration and pH as an acid is diluted tenfold.
questions.modelAnswer: Acid produces H⁺(aq); alkali produces OH⁻(aq). A tenfold dilution reduces H⁺ concentration by factor 10 and increases pH by 1 for a strong acid.
markingPoints: Acid produces H⁺(aq)
alkali produces OH⁻(aq). A tenfold dilution reduces H⁺ concentration by factor 10 and increases pH by 1 for a strong acid.

questions.question: Write the ionic equation for neutralisation and explain what occurs when hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide.
questions.modelAnswer: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l). HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Hydrogen ions from acid combine with hydroxide ions from alkali; sodium and chloride ions are spectators.
markingPoints: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l). HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Hydrogen ions from acid combine with hydroxide ions from alkali
sodium and chloride ions are spectators.

questions.question: Explain the difference between strong and weak acids and between strength and concentration. Compare equal-concentration hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid.
questions.modelAnswer: Strong acid completely ionises in water; weak acid only partially ionises and establishes an equilibrium. Concentration is amount per volume, not degree of ionisation. At equal concentration, HCl has higher [H⁺], lower pH, greater conductivity and usually faster reaction than ethanoic acid.
markingPoints: Strong acid completely ionises in water

weak acid only partially ionises and establishes an equilibrium. Concentration is amount per volume, not degree of ionisation. At equal concentration, HCl has higher [H⁺], lower pH, greater conductivity and usually faster reaction than ethanoic acid.

questions.question: Complete and balance equations for: magnesium + hydrochloric acid; copper oxide + sulfuric acid; calcium carbonate + nitric acid. Name each salt and state the gas tests where relevant.
questions.modelAnswer: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ (magnesium chloride; hydrogen gives squeaky pop). CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O (copper sulfate). CaCO₃ + 2HNO₃ → Ca(NO₃)₂ + H₂O + CO₂ (calcium nitrate; CO₂ turns limewater milky).
markingPoints: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ (magnesium chloride
hydrogen gives squeaky pop). CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O (copper sulfate). CaCO₃ + 2HNO₃ → Ca(NO₃)₂ + H₂O + CO₂ (calcium nitrate
CO₂ turns limewater milky).

questions.question: Describe how to prepare pure, dry copper sulfate crystals from dilute sulfuric acid and insoluble copper oxide. Explain why excess solid is used and why the solution is not heated to dryness.
questions.modelAnswer: Warm dilute acid; add copper oxide in small portions while stirring until some remains/no more reacts; excess ensures all acid is neutralised. Filter to remove excess insoluble oxide. Gently evaporate filtrate to near saturation, cool to crystallise, filter crystals, wash with a little distilled water and dry. Do not heat to dryness because crystals may decompose/lose water and impurities may remain.
markingPoints: Warm dilute acid
add copper oxide in small portions while stirring until some remains/no more reacts

excess ensures all acid is neutralised. Filter to remove excess insoluble oxide. Gently evaporate filtrate to near saturation, cool to crystallise, filter crystals, wash with a little distilled water and dry. Do not heat to dryness because crystals may decompose/lose water and impurities may remain.

questions.question: Describe how to prepare pure, dry sodium chloride crystals from hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide using titration.
questions.modelAnswer: Pipette measured alkali into conical flask; add indicator; add acid from burette while swirling, then dropwise near end point; record titre; repeat to obtain concordant titres. Repeat using exact volumes but without indicator to avoid contaminating crystals. Evaporate to near saturation, cool, filter and dry crystals. Eye-level burette readings and rinsed apparatus improve accuracy.
markingPoints: Pipette measured alkali into conical flask
add indicator
add acid from burette while swirling, then dropwise near end point
record titre

repeat to obtain concordant titres. Repeat using exact volumes but without indicator to avoid contaminating crystals. Evaporate to near saturation, cool, filter and dry crystals. Eye-level burette readings and rinsed apparatus improve accuracy.

questions.question: 25.0 cm³ of sodium hydroxide is exactly neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.150 mol/dm³ sulfuric acid. H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. Calculate the concentration of NaOH.
questions.modelAnswer: Moles H₂SO₄ = 0.150 × 0.0200 = 0.00300 mol. Ratio 1:2, so moles NaOH = 0.00600 mol. Volume NaOH = 0.0250 dm³. Concentration = 0.00600/0.0250 = 0.240 mol/dm³.
markingPoints: Moles H₂SO₄ = 0.150 × 0.0200 = 0.00300 mol. Ratio 1:2, so moles NaOH = 0.00600 mol. Volume NaOH = 0.0250 dm³. Concentration = 0.00600/0.0250 = 0.240 mol/dm³.

questions.question: Explain electrolysis of an ionic compound, including why it must be molten or dissolved, electrode charges, ion movement and oxidation/reduction.
questions.modelAnswer: Electrolysis uses direct current to decompose an electrolyte. Ions must be mobile, so compound is molten or aqueous. Positive ions move to negative cathode and gain electrons (reduction). Negative ions move to positive anode and lose electrons (oxidation). Electrons travel in the external circuit.
markingPoints: Electrolysis uses direct current to decompose an electrolyte. Ions must be mobile, so compound is molten or aqueous. Positive ions move to negative cathode and gain electrons (reduction). Negative ions move to positive anode and lose electrons (oxidation). Electrons travel in the external circuit.

questions.question: Predict the products of molten lead bromide electrolysis and write half equations. State observations.
questions.modelAnswer: Pb²⁺ moves to cathode: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb (reduction); grey/molten lead forms. Br⁻ moves to anode: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ (oxidation); orange-brown bromine gas forms.
markingPoints: Pb²⁺ moves to cathode: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb (reduction)
grey/molten lead forms. Br⁻ moves to anode: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ (oxidation)
orange-brown bromine gas forms.

questions.question: State and apply the product rules for electrolysis of aqueous solutions to: (a) NaCl(aq) with inert electrodes; (b) CuSO₄(aq) with inert electrodes; (c) dilute H₂SO₄.
questions.modelAnswer: Cathode: hydrogen forms unless the metal ion is less reactive than hydrogen. Anode: halogen forms if halide present; otherwise oxygen from hydroxide/water. (a) H₂ at cathode, Cl₂ at anode; NaOH remains. (b) Cu at cathode, O₂ at anode; solution becomes more acidic/paler. (c) H₂ at cathode, O₂ at anode in 2:1 volume ratio.
markingPoints: Cathode: hydrogen forms unless the metal ion is less reactive than hydrogen. Anode: halogen forms if halide present
otherwise oxygen from hydroxide/water. (a) H₂ at cathode, Cl₂ at anode

questions.question: Write balanced half equations for formation of aluminium, copper, hydrogen, chlorine and oxygen during electrolysis.
questions.modelAnswer: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al; Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu; 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ (or 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻); 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻; 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻.

questions.question: Explain the extraction of aluminium by electrolysis, including electrolyte, cryolite, products, half equations, carbon-anode replacement and cost.
questions.modelAnswer: Al₂O₃ is dissolved in molten cryolite, which lowers melting point and energy cost. Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al at cathode. 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ at anode. Oxygen reacts with hot carbon anodes to form CO₂, so anodes wear away and must be replaced. High electricity demand makes process expensive.
markingPoints: Al₂O₃ is dissolved in molten cryolite, which lowers melting point and energy cost. Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al at cathode. 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻ at anode. Oxygen reacts with hot carbon anodes to form CO₂, so anodes wear away and must be replaced. High electricity demand makes process expensive.

questions.question: Describe electrorefining of copper using impure copper and pure copper electrodes in copper sulfate solution. Include electrode changes and half equations.
questions.modelAnswer: Impure copper is positive anode; pure copper is negative cathode. At anode Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻, so it loses mass and impurities form sludge/remain. At cathode Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so pure copper deposits and cathode gains mass. Cu²⁺ concentration remains approximately constant.
markingPoints: Impure copper is positive anode

pure copper is negative cathode. At anode Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻, so it loses mass and impurities form sludge/remain. At cathode Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, so pure copper deposits and cathode gains mass. Cu²⁺ concentration remains approximately constant.

questions.question: Plan an investigation comparing the reactivity of magnesium, zinc and iron with copper sulfate solution using temperature change. Include variables, measurements, repeats, safety and how validity is ensured.
questions.modelAnswer: Independent variable: metal identity. Dependent: maximum temperature rise. Controls: equal mass/moles and surface area of metal, same volume/concentration and starting temperature of CuSO₄, same insulated cup/stirring/time. Measure initial and maximum temperature; calculate ΔT; repeat and mean, identify anomalies. Wear eye protection; copper sulfate harmful. Use excess/consistent limiting reagent and clean metals for validity.

questions.question: Describe an investigation of electrolysis of aqueous sodium chloride using inert electrodes. State observations, tests, hazards and improvements.
questions.modelAnswer: Place inert electrodes in solution connected to d.c. supply; collect gases separately. Cathode bubbles H₂: lit splint squeaky pop. Anode chlorine: bleaches damp litmus after turning it red. Solution near cathode becomes alkaline. Chlorine is toxic: small scale/fume cupboard; eye protection. Keep electrode area, separation, current, concentration and time controlled; rinse apparatus; repeat. Do not mix collected gases.

questions.question: A copper cathode gains 1.27 g in 20 minutes. Explain how increasing current or time affects deposited mass, assuming other factors remain constant.
questions.modelAnswer: Higher current means more charge/electrons pass each second; longer time means charge passes for longer. More Cu²⁺ ions gain electrons, so more copper deposits. Deposited mass is proportional to charge Q = It.
markingPoints: Higher current means more charge/electrons pass each second
longer time means charge passes for longer. More Cu²⁺ ions gain electrons, so more copper deposits. Deposited mass is proportional to charge Q = It.

questions.question: Write ionic equations for: zinc with copper(II) ions; magnesium with hydrogen ions; silver nitrate with sodium chloride. Identify spectator ions in the full equations.
questions.modelAnswer: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu. Mg + 2H⁺ → Mg²⁺ + H₂. Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl. Spectator ions are unchanged on both sides (for example sulfate in first, chloride in Mg/HCl, sodium and nitrate in precipitation).
markingPoints: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu. Mg + 2H⁺ → Mg²⁺ + H₂. Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl. Spectator ions are unchanged on both sides (for example sulfate in first, chloride in Mg/HCl, sodium and nitrate in precipitation).

questions.question: A strong acid changes from pH 2 to pH 4. Calculate the factor change in hydrogen-ion concentration and state the direction.
questions.modelAnswer: Each pH unit is factor 10. Increase of 2 pH units means [H⁺] decreases by 10² = factor 100.
markingPoints: Each pH unit is factor 10. Increase of 2 pH units means [H⁺] decreases by 10² = factor 100.

questions.question: Choose suitable reactants to prepare copper chloride, potassium sulfate and magnesium nitrate, and justify whether excess-solid or titration method is used.
questions.modelAnswer: Copper oxide/carbonate + HCl: insoluble excess-solid method. KOH + H₂SO₄: both soluble, titration. MgO/carbonate + HNO₃: insoluble excess-solid method. Acid determines salt ending.
markingPoints: Copper oxide/carbonate + HCl: insoluble excess-solid method. KOH + H₂SO₄: both soluble, titration. MgO/carbonate + HNO₃: insoluble excess-solid method. Acid determines salt ending.

questions.question: Concentrated potassium bromide is electrolysed using inert electrodes. Predict both products, observations and tests.
questions.modelAnswer: Cathode: hydrogen, bubbles, squeaky pop. Anode: bromine, orange-brown fumes/solution; produced because bromide is a halide. Potassium is not discharged in aqueous solution.
markingPoints: Cathode: hydrogen, bubbles, squeaky pop. Anode: bromine, orange-brown fumes/solution
produced because bromide is a halide. Potassium is not discharged in aqueous solution.

questions.question: A current of 2.0 A passes for 15 minutes. Calculate the charge transferred and explain why doubling the charge doubles metal deposited.
questions.modelAnswer: t=900 s; Q=It=2.0×900=1800 C. Charge measures electrons transferred; twice as many electrons reduce twice as many fixed-charge metal ions, so twice the amount/mass deposits.
markingPoints: Q=It=2.0×900=1800 C. Charge measures electrons transferred
twice as many electrons reduce twice as many fixed-charge metal ions, so twice the amount/mass deposits.

questions.question: Complete and label: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + __ ; Cl₂ + __ → 2Cl⁻.
questions.modelAnswer: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ is oxidation (electron loss). Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ is reduction (electron gain).
markingPoints: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ is oxidation (electron loss). Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ is reduction (electron gain).

questions.question: Explain why a pipette and burette are used in titration, why the flask is swirled, and why acid is added dropwise near the endpoint.
questions.modelAnswer: Pipette transfers accurate fixed volume; burette measures variable delivered volume precisely; swirling mixes reactants; dropwise addition prevents overshooting the endpoint. Read meniscus at eye level.

burette measures variable delivered volume precisely

questions.question: A company can obtain copper by mining high-grade ore or bioleaching waste rock. Compare the methods and give a justified choice.
questions.modelAnswer: Mining is faster/high yield but causes habitat loss, waste, dust and energy use. Bioleaching uses low-grade waste, less digging/energy, but is slow and produces leachate needing control and recovery. Choice depends on time, grade, land and environmental controls; conclusion justified by context.
markingPoints: Mining is faster/high yield but causes habitat loss, waste, dust and energy use. Bioleaching uses low-grade waste, less digging/energy, but is slow and produces leachate needing control and recovery. Choice depends on time, grade, land and environmental controls

questions.question: Explain why aluminium can be extracted by electrolysis but iron can be extracted using carbon.
questions.modelAnswer: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot reduce aluminium oxide; electrolysis is required. Iron is less reactive than carbon, so carbon/carbon monoxide can remove oxygen from iron oxide.
markingPoints: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot reduce aluminium oxide
electrolysis is required. Iron is less reactive than carbon, so carbon/carbon monoxide can remove oxygen from iron oxide.

questions.question: During electrolysis of aqueous sodium chloride, predict the products at both electrodes and justify them.
questions.modelAnswer: Hydrogen forms at the cathode because sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so water/H⁺ is reduced. Chlorine forms at the anode because chloride ions are present and are oxidised: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.
markingPoints: Hydrogen forms at the cathode because sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so water/H⁺ is reduced. Chlorine forms at the anode because chloride ions are present and are oxidised: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.

questions.question: Write ionic and half equations for the reaction between zinc and copper(II) ions.
questions.modelAnswer: Overall ionic: Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu. Oxidation: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻. Reduction: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu.

questions.question: Explain why cryolite reduces the energy cost of aluminium extraction.

questions.question: Explain why a burette is rinsed with the solution it will contain rather than only with water.

questions.question: Explain why the same current and electrolysis time must be used when comparing two electrolytes.
questions.modelAnswer: Charge transferred depends on current × time and affects amount of product. Controlling both makes electrolyte composition the intended independent variable.
